passages.title: Passage 1
passages.instructions:
Questions 1–40

You should spend about 60 minutes on Questions 1–40, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Housing Affordability and Zoning

A Housing affordability crises in many cities feature median prices outpacing wage growth, lengthening commutes, and crowding young adults into shared flats or parental homes. Economists attribute tight supply partly to zoning codes restricting density, mandating parking minimums, and privileging single-family neighbourhoods resistant to change. Developers face lengthy approvals, impact fees, and litigation from homeowners citing property value protection and character preservation. Renters bear burden through rising rents capturing locational amenities without capturing land value gains accruing to owners politicised by local electoral incentives favouring incumbents voting in low-turnout municipal elections dominating land use decisions with regional externalities ignored constitutionally when cities fragmented.

B Inclusionary zoning requires affordable units in new projects or in-lieu fees funding off-site construction, trading cross-subsidy for permission to build market-rate towers. Effectiveness depends on overall supply elasticity; if baseline permissions scarce, mandates may reduce starts. Upzoning near transit stations aims to align climate goals with compact growth, yet backlash mobilises when height shadows feared despite design guidelines mitigating visually in some cases not persuading emotionally attached residents nostalgic for low-rise skylines symbolising status and stability amid perceived threat of anonymous renters and traffic congestion narratives amplified by social media groups coordinating objections flooding planning hearings with repetitive talking points drowning technical staff recommendations based on housing needs assessments quantifying

C Tax policies matter: mortgage interest deductions favour owners, capital gains exclusions encourage holding, while property tax caps like California's Proposition thirteen reduce turnover and homogenise ageing ownership patterns limiting supply responsiveness. Land value taxes theoretically incentivise efficient site use yet remain politically rare. Community land trusts separate ownership of land from buildings, preserving affordability long term through resale formulas. Cooperative housing models pool equity among residents, underutilised in some countries despite success in others. Speculative investment by non-resident buyers inflates prices disconnected from local earnings, prompting foreign buyer taxes and vacancy taxes with mixed evidence depending on enforcement capacity and loopholes via corporate shells obscuring beneficial ownership tracing challenges for

D Construction costs rose with material prices, skilled labour shortages, and safety code upgrades after disasters prompting stricter seismic and fire rules rightly prioritising life safety yet increasing per-unit expenses passed to buyers unless subsidised. Modular and prefabricated methods promise speed yet face financing hurdles and NIMBY stigma associating factory housing with quality fears sometimes outdated. Labour unions negotiate prevailing wage requirements on subsidised projects, trading affordability goals against fair compensation debates ethical not purely technical. Supply chain disruptions during pandemics delayed projects, worsening shortages temporarily, highlighting vulnerability of just-in-time building logistics reliant on imported components when borders close or tariffs shift abruptly amid trade disputes unrelated to housing yet transmitted

E Regional inequality emerges when superstar cities attract talent while others hollow out, a spatial dimension of affordability discussions beyond intra-city zoning. Remote work post-pandemic enabled some outmigration easing pressure modestly yet not uniformly. Federal governments experiment with housing vouchers expanding tenant choice if landlords participate, often limited by discrimination and payment timeliness reputations among small landlords wary of bureaucracy. Public housing histories carry stigma from underinvestment and segregationist siting, complicating new social housing campaigns despite successful Nordic models maintaining quality management and mixed-income integration when funded consistently rather than stigmatised as warehouses for poor isolated from transit and jobs perpetuating cycles planners now seek to break via location-efficient siting criteria

F Environmental reviews sometimes delay infill projects ironically, when densification would reduce sprawl emissions; streamlining procedures without gutting legitimate ecological protections remains contentious. Parking reform reducing mandatory spots lowers costs and car dependence, facing opposition where car storage equated with property rights culturally. Accessory dwelling unit legalisation unlocks backyard flats gently increasing supply in residential blocks if owners finance construction and tenants gain rights against arbitrary eviction simultaneously via just-cause protections debated hotly as trade-off between investor flexibility and renter security in tight markets where displacement fears dominate politics more than abstract efficiency arguments economists prefer yet fail to communicate empathetically to fearful neighbours seeing change as loss not collective gain

G Looking ahead, the author argues affordability requires zoning reform, stable funding for social housing, and anti-speculation tools coordinated regionally. Homeowner vetoes cannot trump regional needs indefinitely without generational inequity hardening into class division. Transparency about who benefits from scarcity—incumbent owners—should inform democratic debate. Pilot upzoning with tenant protections may build coalitions bridging renters and YIMBY activists distrustful of market-only solutions. If cities continue exporting homelessness while blocking apartments, fiscal and moral costs will rise. Balanced packages pairing supply expansion with inclusion, labour standards, and environmental safeguards offer pragmatic path respecting both shelter as human right and legitimate neighbourhood voice without granting universal veto freezing young families out of secure housing
